title: Multiplayer
description: This workshop will explore the multi-faceted world of digital multiplayer environments. We will present an interactive workshop that puts participants in a simulated representation of role creation, identity, and competition. The workshop will be punctuated by talks by panelists on the various ways players affect and are, in turn, affected by these games.

abstracts.title: David Li ~ he/him
abstracts.description:
David Li

Addons in World of Warcraft have evolved from simple interface modifications into powerfultools that reshape how players, and the community, engage with content. Much of bothin-the-moment and coordination decision-making can be off-loaded onto addons to the pointwhere competitive fairness can be called into question. Drawing on prior studies about userinterface modification, as well as Mia Consalvo’s book Cheating, this paper analyzes how whatis fair, cheating, and expected, is negotiated within the WoW community, and how it is enforced,both by players and the developers, Blizzard.

Although the general consensus among players is that addons’ abilities to offload effort onto thecomputer does give an advantage to those who use them, instead of pushing back againstthem, they choose to embrace them, and socially enforce them within their play spaces. Playersexpect their teammates to use addons, just like they do, which can flip the script–now playerswho choose not to use them (or do not know about them) are playing unfairly, as they now holdthe team back from performing at their most optimal.

Very recently, Blizzard attempted to address this unfairness after many years of notacknowledging the imbalance directly, by limiting addon functionality in combat and integratingkey features into the base game. These efforts aim to level the playing field and standardizeaccess to information for all, but it instead exposed the other side of the issue, which pertains toaccessibility and customization. One size fits all leaves players behind, creating a different kindof unfairness. This exposes a careful balance between competitive integrity with accessibility,player expression, and community expectations.

abstracts.title: Faris Kazim
abstracts.description: Faris Kazim

abstracts.title: Matthew Lamm
abstracts.description:
Matthew Lamm

This paper examines toxicity in competitive multiplayer games not as an anomaly ofplayer behavior, but as an emergent property of designed game systems. While toxicity iscommonly framed as individual misconduct, such as the examples of harassment,flaming, or feeding, this research situates it at the intersection of psychological frustration,social structure, and designed mechanics. Focusing on team-based multiplayerenvironment, this study looks at how games produce and sustain toxic behavior, and howwe can use frameworks from other areas of study to instead design for pro-social play.

Drawing from Michel Foucault’ s concept of “docile bodies,” Andrew K. Przybylski’swork on competence frustration, and Pierre Bourdieu’s practice, this research adaptssystems-oriented design analysis and cross-disciplinary frameworks to multiplayer gamedevelopment. Findings suggest that toxicity arises from the interactions betweencompetence-impeding frustration, socially amplified blame within team structures, andaffordances of digital environments. Compared to other game development fields, such asfirst-person-shooters that have decades of iterative and empirical tuning. pro-social designhas had to rely on intuition and reactionary methods. In response, this paper proposesspeculative design interventions that redistribute responsibility, obscure individual failurebehind team accomplishment, and reinforce-prosocial behaviors through systemicincentives rather than reactive moderation.

This research will be presented alongside a live workshop in which participantsengage in a simulated massive multiplayer gaming experience. The workshop will contrastintuition-driven and systemically designed social mechanics, allowing participants toexperience how different rule structures can shape player behavior in real time. Together,this paper and the workshop propose a shift from managing toxicity as an individualphenomenon to intentionally designing for “friendly bodies” through rigorous systemsdesign.

abstracts.title: Rena Chen
abstracts.description:
Rena Chen

The formation of identity is normally driven by social rules and situational context, yetthis process is rarely easy to observe directly. It involves multiple entangled factors andthus unfolds too gradually to be directly examined. This paper argues that MMOs act asa compressed testing ground, where the same mechanisms that shape identity in realsociety operate in a simpler, faster, and more visible way.

The paper first draws on Goffman's performance theory and Milik's concept of personato clarify the non-binary relationship between players and their characters, andtogether with Snodgrass's research, argues that the identities formed in MMOs areextensions of players' real selves rather than purely fictional personas constructed as anescape from reality. Building on this, the paper examines two core systems throughwhich MMOs shape player identity: the class system and the guild system. First, theclass assigns players a structural identity from the moment they enter the game andcontinuously reinforces this through communities. Second, guild structures provideplayers with sustained group belonging and role practice, mirroring how identity isconstructed through organizational membership in real life. Among the aspects, thequantification system makes player contributions public and comparable, giving visibleform to identity practices that would otherwise remain hidden. Through the comparisonamong Jian Wang 3, World of Warcraft, and Final Fantasy XIV, the paper further arguesthat these mechanisms are structural features of the MMO genre rather than isolatedcases.

The paper concludes that MMOs provide a simplified testing ground for social identity,compressing the complexity of real-life identity formation into a more contained andobservable space.

abstracts.title: Riley Lyman
abstracts.description:
Riley Lyman

MMOs are uniquely ephemeral experiences. Any game is liable to be lost to time, butnone so readily as the MMO, whose technical and networking requirements makepreservation efforts a massive challenge. However, this problem cannot be solved byreplicating game data alone. In this paper, I show that an MMO cannot be preservedwithout rich documentation of its social and gameplay dynamics, arguing specificallythat player storytelling best fulfills this preservative role. I demonstrate this by close-reading YouTuber Barny's World of Warcraft videos, analyzing the ways in which herstories convey the intricacies of events that could otherwise never be relived. I thenexpand my analysis outward to show how this same preservative thread traces itsway through player stories about other multiplayer experiences. I contrast theseexamples against single-player Let's Play videos, showing how MMO player storiesare uniquely effective tools for capturing ephemeral social interactions. Unlike single-player games, which can be reexperienced at any time, the experience of an MMO isdependent on the social dynamics produced by a specific cultural context. MMOworlds can and have been rebuilt, whether that be via community-led private serversor official relaunches of once-dead titles. However, even if that world is identical inform to the past, there is no way to replicate the original social interactions to be had.I conclude that story is the only viable method to preserve these intrinsically humanaspects of gameplay.

title: Genre
description: From interactive fiction to open world MMOs, video games can be a myriad of genres. Beneath that diversity lies a question every game must answer: what can the player actually do? This panel explores the relationship between genre, design and player agency. We’ll look at how players interact with the game world in different ways, how the genre sets the rules of that interaction, and what can happen when those rules are deliberately broken. What happens when a narrative game removes your freedom of choice, right at the most crucial moment? Or when a horror game takes away your weapons— just as something in the dark comes out to get you? We focus on designers’ perspective and discuss what are the ways they use to facilitate the agency of the players (or lack thereof), taking deep dives into genres such as psychological horror, crime fiction, and no-input games. Each section opens with an introduction to the genre and its associated player experience patterns, followed by roundtable discussion and Q&A with intermittent audience participation.

abstracts.title: Amber Xia
abstracts.description:
Amber Xia

Psychological horror in video games is frequently misunderstood as a genre defined by whatit withholds, as in no monsters, no jump scares, no explicit violence. Yet this framing fails toexplain why certain games produce a dread that lingers long after play ends, while others thatemploy the same surface-level restraint feel hollow. What specific design mechanisms makepsychological horror in video games effective, and why do some works succeed where othersfail?

This paper argues that psychological horror achieves its greatest effect by engineering acollapse of perceptual and agentive trust. By embedding dread within mundane environmentsand familiar mechanics, and manipulating the imbalance between what players control andwhat they are forced to confront, the player becomes complicit in their own disorientation.Drawing on game studies scholarship concerning player agency, cognitive fear responses,environmental design, and psychoanalytic frameworks of the uncanny and abjection, thispaper examines case studies including Martha is Dead, OMORI, Anatomy, F.E.A.R., andSlender: The Eight Pages to identify three interlocking mechanisms: the environment ashidden horror architecture, the erosion of perceptual trust, and the deliberate imbalance ofagency that produces complicity.

In conclusion, this paper claims that psychological horror is fundamentally a design strategyof misdirection and erosion rather than confrontation, and that when these mechanisms areabsent or over-explained, horror loses its hold on the player entirely. Understanding thesemechanisms offers a framework for both analyzing and designing horror experiences thatoperate invisibly, beneath the surface of play.

abstracts.title: Hansong Li
abstracts.description:
Hansong Li

Player agency is often considered central to digital games, but remains to be inconsistentlydefined in detective mystery games. Many such games try to sell the illusion of being thedetective, but the exact degree of freedom for the player to act within the game world can varydrastically, and sometimes the detective works are merely a narrative flavor instead of concreteverbs. This paper argues that player agency—specifically the abilities and ways to askquestions, interpret information, and verify conclusions—is the genre-defining attribute ofdetective mystery games.

Building on Aarseth’s concept of ergodic literature and subsequent work on interactive agency,this paper develops an analytical framework which examines how agency operates across keyelements of detective gameplay, including information collection, player-world interaction, playerassumption confirmation, mechanism to submit answers and out-of-game cognitive works.

The framework is applied to a range of historically significant titles, from Myst (1993) to Returnof the Obra Dinn (2018). The analysis demonstrates that effective detective design depends noton the number of choices available, but on enabling meaningful epistemic interaction.

Furthermore, based on the findings, the paper explores unexplored possibilities within andbeyond the genre, by taking inspiration from post-modern detective fiction, and tries to examineemerging titles such as Disco Elysium (2019) and Outer Wilds (2019) with this new perspective.

abstracts.title: Jon Topielski
abstracts.description:
Jon Topielski

“Zero Input Games” is a new term for a small subclass of games that require little, if any,input from the player. Some examples include Blaseball (Sam Rosenthal), where players followalong but can’t influence any of the game, or Progress Quest (Eric Frederickson), where playerssimply watch as the simulation unfolds. This presentation discusses how zero-input games canbe included in the conversation on the definition of games. These low-input experiences bearstriking similarity to media in film, books, and other artistic mediums, raising questions aboutwhether similar experiences in other mediums might be analagous to those that we alreadyconsider to be games. In our research, we established a classification criteria for betterunderstanding zero-input games that generate novel possibilities for analysis. Trends arerevealed through this analysis; films that are game-like tend to be of the type that viewers solvein their head and simulations that are game-like tend to be of the type where viewers simplywatch as it unfolds. Based on these findings, two objects were created in mediums that attemptto subvert the typical types of zero-input experiences that is typically present. In doing so, twonovel contributions are made to the burgeoning field of zero-input games and game-like media.

abstracts.title: Kai DeJesus ~ they/them
abstracts.description:
Kai DeJesus

The NBC show The Traitors popularized a reality television show format in which certain eventsthat happened were entirely false: for example, several of the guests being “murdered”, ratherthan being “eliminated” (or “voted off the island”). A reality show with false events is not a newphenomenon. However, some reality television shows, sometimes dubbed “surreality” television,incorporate challenges, scripted scenes, actors, and props to create a mostly unscriptedtelevision experience in which contestants compete to complete a story that couldn’t have beentold otherwise using the reality television format, like isekai. In this study, I examined how realitytelevision shows create game mechanics to carry out actions that characters in a crime fictionstory would do, like investigate and murder. I also examined how the game elements, like thehost and scripted scenes, create characters, a plot, and a setting for the contestants to developa narrative through play. This article defines surreality television and argues that shows that tieplayer performance in individual challenges to monetary reward often create mini-games thatignore the plot in favor of creating an opportunity for the players to increase their potentialwinnings. Surreality television shows that use diegetic challenge formation, in which thecontestants are instructed to carry out tasks in reaction to what a non-player character has done(rather than said) can create a more cohesive crime fiction narrative.

title: Aesthetics
description: In this panel we examine what kinds of stories games tend to tell, how they tell those stories,and why we keep coming back, with a particular focus on violence, power dynamics,mechanical expression, and aesthetics. Join us for a procedurally-generated series of talkscovering the what, why, and how of storytelling in games, followed by an audience-directedroundtable discussion where we put you, the players, in charge.

abstracts.title: Claire Lincoln
abstracts.description:
Claire Lincoln

Video games often make players feel powerful. Players wield awesome abilities, assumethe role of competent heroes, and make meaningful choices. These expressions of power oftenconstruct a fantasy for the player to revel in and are amplified by interactivity, a staple of themedium. Prior research lays the groundwork for interactivity to be a meaningful source of power,awarding players a sense of agency over the experience. This paper operates under theunderstanding that the video game medium is primed and even expected to uphold player agencyand fantasies of power. And, to offer insight into the role of interactivity, this paper explores acollection of games that subvert these fantasies, challenge player agency and recontextualizepower as an undesirable experience.

This paper demonstrates how games like Mouthwashing and Horses challenge playeragency by deliberately restricting player choice and forcing participation in disturbing scenarios.Notably, these are violent games; however, violence is treated not as a justified application ofpower, but rather as a source of discomfort and uncomfortable truths. Silent Hill 2 accomplishesa similar feat, inviting the player into a fantasy only to recontextualize their actions in the game’sfinal moments, stripping away violence’s justification and recasting the hero as weak andculpable. Similarly, other examined titles subvert the appeal of playing a likable and competentcharacter, challenging any sense of power the player may gain through identifying with theiravatar. Agency, rather than a source of empowerment, constructs an experience that is full oftension and reflection, a total subversion of the fantasy players have come to expect.

Ultimately, this paper proposes that video games, through their unique employment ofinteractivity and promise of player agency, are especially effective at critiquing power andviolence. By disrupting traditional power fantasies, these works encourage players to reflect ontheir expectations of control, their desire for power, and the ethics of virtual violence.

abstracts.title: George Eltzroth ~ any
abstracts.description:
George Eltzroth

By now, videogames are well past their infancy. The medium is host to myriad works thatleverage its unique narrative capabilities to tell personal, resonant, and affecting stories. Despitethis, the academic field of game studies, fledgeling though it may be in the context of academia,is far more developed than the related field of game analysis. This is a work of game analysis.The intention of this paper is to name, and define two techniques for storytelling that are uniqueto videogames: emergence and embodiment, and contextualize their place in the greaterlineage of writing and analysis on games, procedurality, and storytelling. I will then examinewhen and how they are employed by playing and analyzing three illustrative games. Those casestudies are: Blaseball, Children of the Sun, and Far: Lone Sails, three games which use thesestorytelling techniques to different extents and with different levels of visibility, creating a broadportrait of how existing games tell stories.

abstracts.title: Zhili Chen
abstracts.description:
Zhili Chen

Violence has long been a central component of game design, yet it is often treated primarilyas a mechanic of challenge or spectacle rather than as a meaningful expressive tool. This project investigates violence as a form of expression in games, asking how violent systemscan convey emotion, character, and narrative rather than merely serve as interactive conflict resolution.

This research contributes to ongoing discourse by reframing violence not as content alone,but as a designed language embedded within player interaction. Drawing from analyses ofexisting games, film theory, and interactive media studies, the project examines how timing,player agency, repetition, and feedback systems shape the emotional and narrative meaningof violent acts. Particular attention is given to how systems of escalation, loss of control, andembodiment can transform violence into a vehicle for expressing psychological states.The practical component of this research is a prototype game that situates combat within theeveryday life of a troubled high school student. In this work, fighting is not the primary goalbut one aspect of a broader simulation, where player actions accumulate toward moments ofloss of control, represented through a “possession” system. This design explores how violencecan emerge from systemic pressure rather than player intention alone.

The findings suggest that when integrated with narrative systems and player state, violencecan function as a powerful expressive medium, capable of communicating internal conflictand social tension. This project demonstrates how recontextualizing violence can expand itsrole within game design beyond spectacle toward meaningful expression.

title: Industry
description: Games are much more than the software we interact with - they’re the people who make them, the corporations greenlighting them, and the financial structures that can both make them possible and interfere with their core design in the same breath. Beginning with individual presentations, this panel will seek to explore each of those topics through a multitude ofperspectives. Destin will talk about the explosion of live-service games in the post-pandemicdigital games industry, connecting a throughline to the eventual mass layoffs that plagued the industry in its wake. Madeline will draw comparisons between the Hollywood film industry andthe modern gaming industry through the lens of its employees: What can we learn from more developed creative industries about how best to protect the people working within it from bothinternal and external harm? Abhi will dive into “gacha” game design and how it stems from theeconomy of time, going deep into the pity system and eventually exploring ways of doing ethical gacha design. Finally, Peyton will bring us into the world of analog gaming, giving an extensive study of Kickstarter through its top 100 board games to discover common trends and form apicture of what a successful campaign might look like in the modern Kickstarter environment.After individual presentations, the entire panel will come together to talk amongst themselves ina roundtable discussion that will afterwards be open to audience involvement.

abstracts.title: Abhishek Chatterjee ~ he/him
abstracts.description:
Abhishek Chatterjee

The 'Free-to-Play' (F2P) mobile games industry is built on a difficult conflict: the desire todesign a fun game versus the pressure to design a profitable product. This tension is mostobvious in Gacha mechanics. Developers often pitch mechanics like the 'Pity System', whichguarantees a drop after a certain number of failed pulls, as a safety net for players. However,critics usually dismiss these systems as predatory gambling. This back-and-forth ignores thecomplex reasons players actually choose to engage with these games and the specific UI tricksused to keep them spending.

This paper bridges the disconnect between industry PR and academic critics by combining mypersonal experience as a former mobile systems designer with academic research. Using afractal approach, the paper first looks at Gacha through the broader 'Economy of Time,'exploring how modern players rationalize spending money just to skip the grind. It thenexamines the core F2P ecosystem, showing how early-game 'fun' pivots into aggressivemonetization once a player becomes a veteran. Finally, it breaks down the specific UI of the PitySystem, showing how it hides real-world costs and weaponizes the player's sunk time.

By applying an ethical framework to these systems, the paper concludes that 'Ethical Gacha' ispossible. It proposes a set of 'Ethical Design Pillars', focusing on absolute transparency andhard financial caps, arguing that sustainable design must respect the player's agency ratherthan relying on deceptive mechanics.

abstracts.title: Destin Piagentini
abstracts.description:
Destin Piagentini

Leading up to the Covid-19 pandemic, the digital gaming industry had enjoyed a period ofcontinued growth in both player acquisition and resource investment. That upward trajectory notonly continued through the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic, but surged as a result of it.While players were stuck at home, it became easier to devote their time to entertainment that wasaccessible from their living rooms. At the same time, corporate relief efforts made expansion lessrisky for the companies steering the industry to pump more resources to meet the expandeddemand as a result of the increased time commitment from its players. Eager to spend funds,industry leaders began to set their sights on live-service games as an emerging trend. Inopposition to the traditional model of digital games as finite experiences, live-service-gamesseek to deliver multiplayer experiences that are meant to be played repeatedly as they evolvethrough seasonal up-dates that add new gameplay variations of the core experience. For gamepublishers, a successful live-service game with ongoing revenue opportunities is an attractiveachievement to pursue, but, because these games rely on massive playerbases to support them(often in lieu of an upfront fee), achieving success in this genre has become increasingly difficultas the most popular games are focused on monopolizing the time of their players. As a result,major publishers such as PlayStation Studios have tried to ensure a “hit” through sheer quantity,betting that an investment made in many life-service projects will yield at least one game thatcan generate the profits they’re seeking. In reality, the high difficulty in achieving success forthese games mean that most projects are either cancelled before or shortly after they are releasedto the public. The resulting pivot in strategy leaves the developers of those projects often withoutjobs or stressed to quickly find a new lucrative project on short-notice.

In my new-games journalism piece, I will directly connect the Covid-19 pandemic to therapid expansion and ensuing deflation of the digital gaming industry through the renewed focuson investments into live-service gaming, giving context by analyzing the emergence of thelive-service trend and examining how the pandemic’s early days served as both a powerful andunsustainable boon to the industry but extracted a heavier toll as the macroeconomicenvironment soured for both consumers and companies. Concluding my findings, I will offer ahumanistic perspective on how these broader trends affect the developers working in thisindustry who are, by and large, caught in the crossfire of rapidly changing corporate mandatesand are often left to suffer the largest consequences of their failure.

In my conference presentation, I will briefly summarize these findings before discussingthem amongst other industry challenges in a panel with my peers.

abstracts.title: Madeline Khare
abstracts.description:
Madeline Khare ~ she/her

Flashing lights, limousines, and iconic outfits: celebrities of the early 2000s seemingly had it all. That is, until the paparazzi told us otherwise. Paparazzi feasted off of disproving the so-called perfect lives of primarily women celebrities, to the point they would do anything to get potentially damaging photos to sell to tabloids. These women were stalked, doxed, even live-streamed at their own homes without permission - all so jealous hate-mongerers could critique them to feel better about themselves. Then, less than a decade later in 2014, Gamergate begins. Gamergate is a misogynistic online harassment campaign attacking several women or nonbinary people who were considered successful in their respective games careers. Anonymous “trolls” on forums like 4chan doxed the targets of Gamergate, allowing others to send violent threats directly to their residences. Fast forward another decade, in the 2020’s, there has been a clear shift in the way paparazzi are regarded among Hollywood professionals and the public eye - where it was once revered to photograph a young celebrity’s underwear as she got out of a limousine, now that is an offense punishable by law in several states. Meanwhile, in the games industry where fewer legal action has been taken, experts predict a second Gamergate is coming. This essay will seek to examine what legal gains Hollywood took in order to protect women from harassment in the workplace, and determine if such legal actions could prove useful in the games industry.

abstracts.title: Peyton Schwiebert
abstracts.description:
Peyton Schwiebert ~ he/him

What are the commonalities between the most successful tabletop kickstarters of alltime? What does a modern kickstarter look like in comparison to the original concept of theplatform? What attracts people to crowdfunding games? To answer these questions, researchtook the form of a spreadsheet compiling together data about the top board games on thecrowdfunding website, kickstart, and subsequent data about the game from the website boardgame geek, a compiler of player opinion and wiki resource for all things tabletop. By compilinginformation about the top 100 most successful tabletop games on kickstarter, commonalities ingenre, theme, timing, and attachment to other intellectual properties, along with other factors,can be found. This trend towards prebuilt fanbases in particular shows a change in kickstarterfrom a indie game crowdfunding platform into almost a new form of preorder website, allowinglarger companies to use FOMO on limited time objects to gain more money from the consumer.This can be seen in comparison who has run these kickstarters, and contrasting the price of a“base” game to the average amount donated by backers in order to get limited time add ons.Finally, the research is concluded through an averaging of all of the common attributes in orderto create the next (potential) top 100 kickstarter campaign.

title: Systems
description: This panel discusses the concept of a 'reset' existing across multiple facets of videogames explored through communication, space, time loops, and roguelike mechanics.Our panel consists of four individual brief presentations followed by Q & A sessionsand a joint game design workshop to illustrate our topics.

abstracts.title: Alexander Machalicky
abstracts.description:
Alex Machalicky ~ he/him

While roguelite games began as offshoots of the popular game Rogue, in the modern day,they have become a much more prevalent genre. These types of games often focuson replayability as their main appeal as opposed to other design aspects, making use of limiteddevelopmental resources by allowing them to be reused. This presentation will analyze how afocus on replayability makes it an ideal genre for indie game developers, as well as how thistrend is able to be used within larger projects as well. Through researching the variousdevelopment cycles of roguelites within the indie space such as Hades and Mewgenics, as wellas direct producer testimony from KILLBEAT (Kammonen, 2025), it can be seen that addingelements that enhance replayability to the gameplay loop overall improve the player experience.These will be looked at in conjunction with other analyses which support the notion ofreplayability being a boon to not only roguelites, but to the video game space as a whole (Varga,2025). With all of this in mind, the rationale behind why the roguelite scene has prospered for solong is evident, with the relative absence of developmental resources forcing these types ofgames into making the best possible use of what is at hand. Their focus on replayability issomething that well-established studios ought to be taking note of, potentially utilizing them orotherwise giving support to projects of this type.

abstracts.title: Ashley Newell
abstracts.description:
Ashley Newell ~ she/her

Online multiplayer video games face a worrying challenge: their own communities are pushingplayers away through hostile behaviors. This article discusses developer-driven solutions to theimmensely, socially toxic behaviors present in online multiplayer games driven by bothpsychological and game-mechanics findings. The most common player motivations for socialengagement include playing with existing friends, engaging in cooperative teamplay, andsocializing with new groups, all of which include cooperative engagement to be found to strengthenprosocial tendencies among players towards both game partners and strangers beyond the gameitself. In line with these findings, the most used social features include friend lists, cooperativein-game mechanics, emotes, and spectator options. Whilst the most effective social tools fordiscouraging negative behaviors are those which enable players to both praise and report oneanother for their behavior – a practice known as tootling – as well as placing accountability ontogroups at large rather than individuals, known as the good behavior game. Concerning gamemode, research found that creativity-driven modes encourage greater personal conversationsamong players whilst competitive modes lead to greater nonverbal communication such aslaughing. Through understanding the social and mechanical components that impact theinterpersonal experience of players within online multiplayer games, game creators can shape the types of discussions that take place within their communities, encourage psychological prosocialbehaviors, and implement features that are shown to have the greatest impact on socialengagement. From this research, I will propose a framework through which developers mayminimize social friction and maximize positive social engagement within their games.

abstracts.title: Jiayu Ruan
abstracts.description:
Jiayu Ruan ~ she/her

This research investigates how level design in competitive multiplayer First-Person-Shooters (FPS)with attack-and-defense mechanics contributes to competitive balance while also creating strategic depthfor players with varying levels of skill and game knowledge. The study begins with a review of relevantliterature on level design, spatial organization, and balance in competitive games. Based on this review, amethodology will be developed to analyze zoning structures within selected game levels. Zoningdiagrams will be used to identify the strategic and material composition of these spaces and to examinethe spatial options available to players. A comparative analysis will then be conducted to identify sharedpatterns and key differences across levels from different games. In addition, a heat map of one level fromOverwatch will be produced to visualize how players of different ranks navigate and utilize the samespace. By comparing this heat map with the results of the zoning analysis, the study will evaluate whetherpatterns of player behavior align with the spatial logic and intended strategic functions of the level. Theresearch ultimately aims to formulate level design principles for creating balanced and strategically richcompetitive environments in multiplayer FPS games with attack-and-defense mechanics.

abstracts.title: Xingyu Qin
abstracts.description:
Xingyu Qin ~ she/her

Video games have dual temporality: the time experienced by characters inside the story and thetime experienced by players. As players’ experience of failure, repetition, and learning is notnecessarily reflected in their character, ludonarrative disharmony can become a problem. Time loops as thenarrative structure and mechanics in video games can bridge this gap.

Using the framework of Lahdenperä, this paper first identifies how time loops as a game conceptrefer to the combination of diegetic and extradiegetic level time loops. Based on this category,this paper uses the ludic subjectivity typology developed by Vella and analyzes the case studygames of Ranging Loop, 12 Minutes, and Outer Wilds, pointing out that most time-loop gamesemploy single-embodied ludic subjectivity.

Supported by this subjectivity model, time loop games strengthen players’ sense of identity andbuild emotional connections between players and characters by integrating Mittel’s four types ofcharacter arcs. It demonstrates that time loop mechanics uniquely integrate character overhaul,education, growth, and transformation in ways that mirror players' own mechanical progression,culminating in a shared finale that resolves both narrative and gameplay challengessimultaneously. Therefore, highly aligned character-player arcs created by diegetic andextradiegetic time loops strengthen players’ sense of identity in the single-embodied model andenhance the emotional impacts, constituting a healthy ludo-narrative harmony practice.

This research analyzes time loops as narrative and mechanic tools and contributes acharacter-player arc framework to existing discourse on ludonarrative disharmony. It aims toprovide scholars and designers with a transferable model for analyzing and building cohesiverelationships between game mechanics and storytelling.

title: Makers and Breakers: How the Formats of Game Creation are Intentionally Broken to Create New Possibilities
description: Games get “broken” in many ways. Designers push platforms to their limits to defy genre and tell stories in innovative ways and players break games themselves to upend gameplay. In our presentations and roundtable, we will travel from early internet games to modern queer and trans creators, from autobiographical stories to speedrunners that tell their own stories with someone else’s game, and glimpses into Afrofuturistic game development. We’ll have a moderator help us dive into these topics, how they relate, and what designers can take away from how their games are actually played.

abstracts.title: Finlay Logan
abstracts.description:
Finaly Logan ~ they/them

Discussions of games by marginalized creators consider them in relation to mainstream audiences or in terms of their potential social impact. Terms like “empathy games” and “serious games” highlight games’ capacity to be a catalyst for change, while discourse about queer games as assimilation or as resistance situate these works within the LGBTQ+ community’s struggle for equal rights.

These frameworks, while important for giving games by queer and trans creators increased visibility and critical attention, also risk establishing labels and binaries that further marginalize narratives that don’t fit into those established categories.

Thus, it is necessary to find ways of discussing queer games on their own terms, giving precedence to the relationship that the game establishes between designer and player.

This paper uses Taylor McCue’s game, He Fucked the Girl Out of Me (HFTGOOM) (2022), as a case study to explore this issue. HFTGOOM is a semi-autobiographical game that, although depicts topics of broad socialsuch as transgender identity and sex work, is better understood within the context of McCue’s personaljourney to move past trauma from these experiences.

By analyzing the gameplay and text of HFTGOOM, reading interviews with the developer to learn about the game’s development history and context, and reading both critical and informal player feedback, I show thatexisting frameworks are insufficient to describe this game’s personal impact and significance to the individuals who made and played it.

abstracts.title: Selah Wright
abstracts.description:
Selah Wright ~ she/her

In autobiographical games, the designer constructs a version of themselves as a playable character to ‘play’ a personally lived experience of the designer. These games are unique in the context of gaming and in the broader context of artistic depictions of the self: instead of reacting to the art, the player is asked to act as the creator. Because of this, games require the technical commitment to determine the cause and effect of the players actions. This constraint forces the designer to identify and reconstruct what is in their opinion the fundamental truths of their experiences as well as the critical decisions that led to the outcomes they encountered. As a result, the design decisions of an autobiographical game reflect a thorough self-examination where the finished product reflects the conclusions the designer has reached about a prior experience that they may not have explored otherwise. The aim of this work is to examine how the medium of games influences the designers' understanding and relationship to their personal experiences. Using Stefan Werning’s framework of the procedural persona and Michel Foucault’s technologies of the self, this work will explore how autobiographical games are unique in their impact on self examination. Through the close examination of documented design decisions from two major autobiographical games, Consume Me and He Fucked the Girl Out of Me, this project will analyse how the agency (or lack of) afforded to the player by the designer functions as the embodiment of the designer’s understanding of their personal experience. The result of this work will be a continuation of the framework for understanding autobiographical games not as just novel indie projects but as a distinct evolution in the long tradition of humans making art to understand themselves.

abstracts.title: Stephen Rubino
abstracts.description:
Stephen Rubino ~ he/him

The late 90’s and early 2000’s framed an era poised for technological change, and several influential elements of modern digital culture were formed during this time. While many of these, including several social media sites, still exist and continue to influence digital games and media, Adobe Flash was hugely influential while eventually falling into obsolescence.

In this paper, I apply the approach outlined in Minor Platforms in Videogame History (Nicoll, 2025) to better understand Flash’s place in the development of the interactive web. Flash is situated at what Nicoll refers to as a “moment of rupture” within the gaming world, inhabiting and even facilitating a transition between distinct eras of games, developers, and technological possibilities. We are then able to use Nicoll’s lens to evaluate the ways in which Flash “articulate[d] alternative structures of feeling” and gave rise to unrealized cultural patterns. Namely, we are able to draw connections between Flash and several trends that persist ingaming. These include the rise of “rockstar” indie devs, many of whom came from traditionally outsider career paths and got their start by making games in Flash. It is also possible to chart the beginnings of a trend towards free, browser-based games, starting with influential sites like Newgrounds and culminating in a modern ubiquity of games across non-gaming media.

abstracts.title: Whit Walton
abstracts.description:
Whit Walton ~ they/him

African Diasporic cultures are deeply underrepresented in video games, but this is a part of a larger problem. Colonialism, a violent act of conquering and creating economy out of the lives and bodies of African people, has lasting negative effects in access to education, resources, and global representation. However, African Diasporic people have been able to create with these limitations in place.

From the at-home video game console to the President of Xbox, the contributions to the video game industry are far and wide. However, the games being created are still representative of a white, male, hegemonic view. This is harmful to players, developers, and the global view surrounding African Diasporic people who face discrimination in systemic ways in tandem with avenues of play. By decolonizing the minds of video game developers and encouraging new developers to create stories that resonate with their African Diasporic culture, new code that is void of harmful stereotypes and misconstructions of African people in games can be written.

My research will begin with the history around the Trans-Atlantic slave trade that displaced Africans in the Americas and the innovative creators of technology post-emancipation. Next, it will focus on the current programs created to encourage Black boys to become game testers and current trailblazers in the industry. Finally, I will imagine an Afrofuturistic-inspired game design world. As the future begins to embrace wider technology, video games as emerging media is an industry that can be the preservation of African Diasporic cultures and histories via the African Diasporic game developers who are coming into the field.

title: Couch, 9:16, Shoes, Acrylic Charm
description: What is outside the screen? A couch, 9:16, shoes, and an acrylic charm. What does that have to do with games? In this series of presentations, we will be touching upon what tangents upon the globe of games. Marco Carenza will speak on the uniquely important role that community plays in fighting games; Jingwen Shi will reveal what fuels the popularity of casual games; Ahmed Shuwehdi will analyze museums as walking simulators; finally, Nic Kim will criticize the pitfalls inherent to personal identification through fandom. Following the presentations, we will hold a Q&A with the audience!

abstracts.title: Ahmed Shuwehdi
abstracts.description:
Ahmed Shuwehdi ~ he/him

This paper examines the conceptual and experiential overlap between museums and walking simulators, two seemingly distinct forms of curated environments. While museums have traditionally been framed as spaces of passive observation and education, and walking simulators as a contested genre within video games, both rely on spatial navigation, environmental storytelling, and visitor interpretation as core mechanisms of engagement. The central question of this study is how the design principles of walking simulators can inform and enhance museum experiences while looking at The National Museum of African-American History and Culture as a case study of how a successful implementation could elevate the experience.

This paper contributes to ongoing discussions in museum studies and game design by framing museums as analog counterparts to walking simulators, emphasizing their shared ethos of guided exploration and meaning-making. Drawing on journalistic analysis, critical game studies, and design research, including Mintchev’s museology research on applying video game design to museum exhibits, this study synthesizes concepts such as pacing, environmental storytelling, and player agency.

The paper concludes that integrating walking simulator design principles into museum contexts can transform exhibitions into better participatory experiences without compromising their educational mission. Ultimately, it argues that museums and walking simulators share a foundational logic and that recognizing this relationship opens new possibilities for rethinking how cultural spaces are designed and experienced.

abstracts.title: Marco Carenza
abstracts.description:
Marco Carenza ~ he/him

This paper explores how fighting games foster community in comparison to other competitive games. I will discuss fighting games as a genre and their history and try to redefine what the genre is while giving examples of sub-genres. After establishing the field of study, this analysis will focus on the Fighting Game Community (FGC) as a genre, comparing it to other competitive communities in the gaming space. This analysis finds that while other genres tend to foster their communities online, fighting games have had less official online support. Due to the recency of serviceable online play, fighting games and their communities tend to center on “offline” play spaces, which separates it from other genres. Other games tend to foster more “online” communities, as online play is more convenient. Based on this comparison, I discuss how the FGC values their unique culture and emphasis on social competition.

abstracts.title: Nic Kim
abstracts.description:
Nic Kim ~ he/him and she/her

This zine describes the phenomenon in which fandoms that identify as progressive, safe spaces and are full of minority groups will nonetheless exhibit the same tendency to deny, excuse, or defend bigotry within the fandom's source material and/or the fan communities themselves. In the contemporary, character-centric environment of fandom, this tends to manifest as overwhelming interest in gay male characters – canon or interpreted – juxtaposed with a marked lack of enthusiasm for women characters, characters of marginalized genders, and characters of color. The same anti-change rhetoric present in First-Person-Shooter (FPS) lobbies is replicated in the progressive fandom space, the difference being that gay men are no longer common points of critique. I researched the dominant fanfiction site Archive Of Our Own for data on the relative popularity of characters and found that not only did M/M vastly outperform F/F, but male characters also had more fanfiction written about them in general. The same goes for white characters versus characters of color. I also examined various fandoms such as Disco Elysium, Dropout TV, The Pitt, and Baldur’s Gate 3 for their reactions to political criticisms of their source materials.

I believe it reveals something about how western audiences perceive media consumption: media consumption becomes an identifier, and, moreover, a political identifier. Buying apparel, stickers, and acrylic charms at conventions is reframed as supporting local queer, woman-owned businesses. When one hinges their political identity to the type of games they play, there is an incentive to then defend those games as politically correct, with little room for criticism.

title: Identity
description:
Our panel will be discussing how certain concepts are represented in games and why they’re represented that way. Each panelist will be covering a different aspect of the self and examining how players explore said aspects in and outside of games.

To start, we will have the audience play a version of HARVL, a social deduction game with roleplaying elements. This will contextualize our identity-focused presentations.

Esteban will use the affordances of role-playing games to understand why Facebook’s version of the Metaverse was largely unsuccessful. Though many RPGs – from tabletop to MMOs – already provide a safe and shared space for personal expression, what is the role of technology in creating 'limitless' social worlds?

Mars will examine the Bioshock series to analyze how the heroic father protagonist and the systematic erasure/demonization of motherhood does not necessarily celebrate fatherhood — rather, 'exceptional' male parenting is simply ordinary maternal expectations rebranded as “heroism”.

Lucas will draw on the principles of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy as a lens to explore how mental illness can be taught and represented in games withou the stigma and horror tied to it. He will develop a framework and apply it to examine how Depression Quest portrays the struggles of depression not through psychological horror imagery, but through its procedural rhetoric.

Despoina/DLC will discuss representation of gender in nonhuman characters and analyze how it leads to gender and identity play in Pokémon fans both in-game and IRL. She will examine cosplay, in particular Pokémon cosplay drag (PokeDrag), as a way in which queer Pokemon fans co-opt and co-create the identities of these creatures alongside the designers.

We will conclude with a brief Q&A session with all panelists. The audience will be asked to allow their HARVL roles to guide how they behave duringthe Q&A!

abstracts.title: Despoina/DLC
abstracts.description:
Despoina/DLC ~ she/her

Pokémon, first released during 1996 in versions Red, Green, and later Blue, is a well-beloved video game and transmedia franchise that has amassed all kinds of fans over its 30-year-and-counting lifetime. This presentation aims to discuss the evolution of gender and identity play among Pokémon fans. To that end, I examine five major design choices that have been made to dictate how gender is represented in the Pokémon world. These are:

● 1996-Now: The introduction and function of Pokémon gender as a mechanic

● 2000/2001: The ability to choose the gender of your player character

● 2013: The ability to customize your character avatar

● 2016-2019: The introduction of the first non-binary Pokémon trainer in Pokémon GO

● 2025: The advent of gender-neutral clothing in Pokémon Legends: ZA, Pokémon’s latest main series title

My investigation of these features leads me to observe one way Pokémon fans transition their in-game gender and identity play to the physical world. Irefer to the growing Pokémon cosplay drag (or simply, PokéDrag) scene, found in New York City and other cities with vibrant drag communities. Research done to support this analysis includes interviews with queer Pokémon fans, as well as academic writing on cosplay/drag, Pokémon, and gender representation in games, and the role of Pokémon fan works. This is all in service of my argument that queer Pokémon fans deepen their relationship with the source material and, by extension, themselves, by co-opting and co-creating the identities of these non-human characters.

My conference contribution will feature a presentation that functions as a scoped down version of the larger video essay and will conclude with a PokéDrag performance from yours truly to further contextualize my thesis.

abstracts.title: Esteban Romero
abstracts.description:
Esteban Romero ~ he/him

The Metaverse is a vision of a digital universe popularized in 2021 after Facebook rebranded itself and announced it as their next social platform. They claimed that people could do anything together in this digital universe – from business to education. A few years later, the company is downscaling their Reality Labs division and their proprietary VR social app, Horizon Worlds, has been called 'dead' by major media outlets. In this work, I will analyze the Metaverse beyond its technical challenges to understand its failure as a vision and a culture: a 'technofuturistic dream' of a post-racial, hyper-connected, and limitless VRutopia. By comparing this ideal to the worlds of role-playing games, I support the thesis that the metaverse was largely unsuccessful because it was pitched as away for people to perform real-world activities and lacked the social structures afforded by rules. RPGs, on the contrary, tend to provide a safe and isolated space for play, socialization, emergent storytelling, and identity expression. Through our creativity and capacity for social negotiation, we can use games to transformany social experience into a shared fantasy. This leads me to conclude that a part of Meta’s original vision already exists in the context of RGPs and it can be realized without the need for technology.

abstracts.title: Lucas Chan
abstracts.description:
Lucas Chan ~ he/him

Through the lens of CBT, representing depression through procedural rhetorics can destigmatize mental health and teach players how it feels to have depression froma cognitive and behavioural viewpoint.

Mainstream games that tackle topics of mental illness frequently depict them negatively, associating them with fear and violence. Conversly, while indie games are praised for their more authentic depictions, they are also vulnerable to the same stigmatization due to strong ties with the psychological horror genre. Horror techniques such as jump scares, atmospheric tension, and uncanny aesthetics risk destabilizing players rather than encouraging them to empathize and ultimately undermine the player’s capacity to engage with the game.

This raises questions: What can games do to foster self-reflection and empathy? How can games accurately convey the cognitive and behavioral experience of mentall illness? How do we design games to communicate this without resorting to horror tropes? To address these questions, this paper applies the core principles of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy to analyze how games can utilize mechanics to convey procedural rhetorics about mental health. It then draws comparisons between the structure of treating mentally ill patients in each CBT session and player behavior. This framework is subsequently applied to a case study of Depression Quest (Quinn, 2013) to demonstrate that, through the lens of CBT, it offers a viable model for conveying depression through procedural rhetorics and can destigmatize the negative associations of mental health games.

abstracts.title: Mars So
abstracts.description:
Mars So ~ she/her

Within video game narratives, the trope of the glorified father figure has been a popular choice, as seen in titles ranging from The Last of Us to God of War. And yet, despite the many options for audiences to playas these heroic fatherly characters, the same cannot be said for their maternal counterparts, who are instead typically made absent, if not outright demonized. Taking this into consideration, this paper aims to examine the Bioshock series as a case study to analyze how the heroic father protagonist can only exist through the systematic erasure or demonization of motherhood. To do this, this paper will draw on Shannon Lawlor’s concept of Essential Paternal Masculinity, alongside similar feminist analyses on videogames, to demonstrate how games have been repackaging traditionally maternal qualities as “exceptional” when portrayed by paternal characters. When used to analyze Bioshock’s characters, this further reveals how father-daughter dynamics (such Jack and the Little Sisters, Subject Delta and Eleanor Lamb, and Booker and Elizabeth) are only elevated when their respective maternal figures (Dr. Tenembaum, Sophia Lamb, and Lady Comstock) are either cast as monsters or made absent. By exposing this flaw within the narrative of heroic paternal characters in Bioshock, this paper also aims to highlight the flaw within the trope as a whole, showcasing how similar video games don’t necessarily celebrate fatherhood entirely. Rather, they reveal how “exceptional” male parenting is simply ordinary maternal expectations rebranded as “heroism”.
